FinanceTab.title: How much is the minimum wage going up by?
FinanceTab.text:
The official minimum rates of pay will rise for 2.3 million workers on 1 April.

The rate for workers aged 21 and over is called the National Living Wage, while those aged 18 to 20 are paid the National Minimum Wage. They will both go up by 3.9% next year.

The rates apply across the UK.

From 1 April 2027, workers over 21 on the National Living Wage will be paid £13.21p per hour, up 50p from the current £12.71 an hour.

For someone working full time (35 hours a week), that means an increase of £910 to their gross annual earnings, according to the Treasury.

The rate for 18 to 20-year-olds will rise to £11.27 an hour from 1 April, up from £10.85. For someone working full time, that means an increase of £760 to their gross annual earnings.

The minimum wage for 16 and 17-year-olds is also rising by 3.9%, increasing from £8 an hour to £8.31.

However, these figures mean, this time around, there's no progress on Labour's manifesto promise to narrow the gap in minimum wages between older and younger workers.

There are different rates of pay for apprentices, external depending on their age and what stage of apprenticeship they are in.

Apprentices aged 16 to 18 are entitled to the National Minimum Wage rate for that age group. This is currently £8 an hour but will rise by 3.9% to £8.31 in April.

Those aged 19, or in the first year of their apprenticeship, are paid the same amount.

But those over 19 - or who have already completed their first year - are entitled to the appropriate National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage rate for their age.

Some workers do not qualify for either the National Minimum Wage or the National Living Wage.

This includes the self-employed, company directors, volunteers, members of the armed forces and prisoners.

People with disabilities or in long-term unemployment who take part in government work programmes are paid fixed amounts at different stages of the scheme.

These are less than the equivalent National Minimum or Living rate.

Yes. It is a criminal offence for employers not to pay the correct National Minimum and Living Wages to eligible employees.

The rates apply even if workers are not paid by the hour.

If you think you are being paid the wrong amount, you can complain via the HMRC website, external.

You can also get advice from workplace experts Acas, external.

FinanceTab.title: Workers should be able to know colleagues' salaries, rights body says
FinanceTab.text:
Employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning, the UK's equality watchdog has said.

Bosses should be required to respond to questionaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has proposed, external.

In addition, employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from carrying on, it said.

Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them.

At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about colleagues.

The EHRC urged lawmakers to make it compulsory for employers to provide information including colleagues' basic pay and hours worked, how employees' pay compares with each other, and information about bonuses, overtime, shift-premiums and performance-related pay, within a specific timeframe.

The rights watchdog argued that this would help cut pay discrimination, especially against women.

FinanceTab.title: US midterm elections: Trump's biggest economic problem looks familiar
FinanceTab.text:
The White House is confronting a familiar dilemma. The economic numbers aren't necessarily bad - but the public mood is.

It's a disconnect that haunted Joe Biden in 2024, when solid headline data failed to convince many voters that the economy was working for them.

Now, Donald Trump faces a version of the same challenge.

During the 2024 campaign, Trump promised voters swift relief from rising prices.

"When I win, I will immediately bring prices down," he said.

Delivering on that promise has proved harder than expected.

Economic growth is holding up, unemployment remains low and the stock market is near record highs.

Yet the final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections confirms what voters already know: prices remain high.

The causes are different. Biden was grappling with the aftermath of the Covid pandemic. Trump faces higher energy prices linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran and the fallout from some of his own trade and immigration policies.

The political reality, however, is much the same. Voters are not judging the economy by GDP figures or record highs on the stock market. They are judging it by what they pay at the supermarket, petrol prices and whether they can keep up with the bills.

US economic growth of 2.2% would be respectable by the standards of many wealthy economies. Germany, for example, has struggled to generate comparable momentum. And a stable US unemployment rate of 4.2% hardly suggests an economy in freefall.

Trump argues that he inherited an economic mess from Biden, and points to strong growth, investment and stock market performance as evidence that his policies are working.

Following the most recent inflation report, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said the administration's "aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda" had blunted "Biden's inflation crisis".

Larry Kudlow, a Trump ally and economic commentator, has described the current expansion as "the greatest story never told", external, arguing that "nobody is getting fired".

The impact might have been larger if Trump hadn't later paused some tariffs, struck new trade deals and been blocked by the Supreme Court from using emergency powers to impose many others.

Then came another shock. Conflict with Iran pushed oil prices higher, lifting the cost of petrol and putting fresh pressure on household budgets.

The White House points to tax cuts, job growth and lower prescription drug costs as evidence that the administration is delivering for American families. And it is increasingly embracing policies aimed at easing pressures.

Trump has called for a cap on credit card interest rates and floated the idea of a $5,000 payment to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress.

The measures reflect a political reality familiar to both parties: when voters are anxious about prices, arguments about solid growth and low unemployment are rarely enough.

Biden never found a way to bridge the gap between economic performance and economic sentiment. The question heading into the midterms is whether Trump can.

If recent political history is any guide, perceptions of the economy may matter more than the economic data itself.

FinanceTab.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
FinanceTab.text:
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.

The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".

It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (£6,000) from $1,800.

Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".

"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.

The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.

There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres.

The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.

Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.

The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.

Passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told the BBC they were informed by Villa Vie Residences' chief executive at 6am on Tuesday that they had to leave by 2pm on the same day.

The couple said passengers had known for some time about the company's financial difficulties. A potential investor had previously come onboard the ship to do due dilligence, but in the end it did not work out.

"Even then, we were still hoping a miracle investor would come through," they said. "Although there were signs that this would happen, we still felt disbelief when it became real. We were heartbroken. It felt like our dream had been crushed."

"There have been a lot of hugs and tears as residents support one another and process what has happened."

Another passenger Holly Hennessey said that the ship's passengers had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".

Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said.

"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," Hennessey told the BBC from Cambodia.

"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting."

Canen and Bodin said the location in Cambodia was "a difficult place to disembark" because of the distance to a major international airport.

FinanceTab.title: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
FinanceTab.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.

The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.

Anthropic also detailed some of the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.

Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.

Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.

Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.

"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.

It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.

But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".

One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.

Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.

The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.

Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.

The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.

Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.

Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.

"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.

Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.

At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.

Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.

Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.

The leasing of data centres alone is set to cost the company $321.4bn through agreements struck so far this year.

Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.

Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.

Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.

A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10m in the past year.

An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.

Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".

The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.

Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.

Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.

Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".

The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.

For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.

"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.

That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."

"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission."

Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice, and making more efficient power grids and batteries.

Anthropic said AI could one day provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.

"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

FinanceTab.title: Data centre backlash grows ahead of US midterms - here's what you need to know
FinanceTab.text:
Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.

These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.

They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.

But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.

In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.

It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.

Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.

There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map, external, a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.

That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000, external operational sites.

As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.

Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.

FinanceTab.title: Live Updates: Fed Expected to Hold Rates Steady Even as Inflation Pushes on Prices
FinanceTab.text:
In recent weeks, the White House has redoubled its efforts to oust Lisa D. Cook, a Fed governor, over allegations of mortgage fraud that she has consistently denied. The matter is set to come to a head on Nov. 5, when the administration aims to grill Ms. Cook at an unorthodox, private hearing that her lawyers have said is politically tainted.

Caught in the middle is Mr. Warsh, who has tried to walk a fine line between defending the Fed’s independence, maintaining a good relationship with the president and steering clear of one of the most sensitive issues ever to face his institution. His next steps will carry great weight, given the stakes for the nation’s central bank and its more than century-old mission to set monetary policy free from political influence.

For the moment, Ms. Cook’s fate is unclear. Her lawyers told the White House she could not appear for the November hearing, citing scheduling conflicts and foreign travel. Since then, her lawyers and White House officials have repeatedly declined to say if they were discussing moving the different hearing date or another option entirely.

Nevertheless, the hearing itself is an outgrowth of Mr. Trump’s first attempt to fire Ms. Cook, which she successfully sued to block in a case that reached the Supreme Court. In a June ruling, the justices took no position on the charges against her, but they did say that Mr. Trump should have afforded Ms. Cook a proper chance to respond to them.

Throughout that drama, Mr. Warsh has largely refrained from commenting on the charges against his colleague — or on the president’s general attempts to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates.

At one point during his confirmation hearing to become chairman, Mr. Warsh was explicitly asked about Ms. Cook’s lawsuit against the president. It had named the Fed board as well as Jerome H. Powell, then the leader of the central bank, as defendants, citing the fact that the Fed could have been required to carry out the firing.

Asked if as chairman he would defend Ms. Cook’s tenure, Mr. Warsh revealed little about his thinking.

“If I stand for anything, it’s the Fed should stay in its lane,” he said, citing the fact that the case at that time had not yet been decided.

He added: “It’s inappropriate for me to weigh in on that, especially because, in the event that I am confirmed, I could be a party to that matter.”

Although Ms. Guity, 33, and her husband want to own their own home in the area, buying would be too much of a financial stretch as long as mortgage rates remained high. The possibility that a monthly mortgage payment would exceed $6,000 was enough to convince her that her family would stay renters for much longer than she had once thought.

“We’re depending on the graces of the landlord,” she said.

Higher mortgage rates are compelling aspiring homeowners across the country to continue renting, tightening competition for rentals and putting upward pressure on rents for the first time in years. According to private-sector data from real estate sites including Zillow and Apartment List, rents have steadied in recent months after a prolonged softening driven by a glut in new apartment buildings that sprouted up after the pandemic. Government data also show sturdier rent growth.

Annual change in prices for “rent of primary residence”

The upswing in rents could pose a challenge for the Federal Reserve in its fight against persistent price increases. Though the Fed is expected to hold rates steady at its meeting on Wednesday, investors anticipate the central bank will raise borrowing costs once more before year-end, which would keep mortgage rates elevated.

“We’re not in deceleration world anymore, probably not going to get a lot of disinflationary pressures from rents,” said Jonathan Millar, senior U.S. economist at Barclays. “If anything, the risks are that we may be going the other direction.”

The emerging signs of strength in the rental market follow a roller coaster of a period. During the depths of the pandemic, housing demand soared, fueled by a desire for more space, the ability to work from home and swelling savings. Without the supply to match, both home prices and rents skyrocketed in much of the country.

That demand for housing, coupled with rock-bottom interest rates, encouraged residential builders to flood growing cities, especially in the Sun Belt, with new rental properties. The mushrooming housing stock, along with generous incentives to attract renters, decreased landlords’ pricing power and compelled them to slash rents rapidly in many big cities nationwide. Rents in cities including Austin, Texas, and Phoenix plummeted in the years after the pandemic.

Then rising interest rates starting in 2022 made it more expensive to finance large construction projects, which slowed the building frenzy. Tariffs and supply chain troubles have pushed up material costs, and a labor shortage, exacerbated by President Trump’s immigration policy, has also weighed on construction. Higher mortgage rates and lofty home prices are making home buying increasingly inaccessible for a vast number of people. Homeowners who secured ultralow rates during the depths of the pandemic are reluctant to sell, further slowing the housing market.

At the same time, the labor market, which has been characterized by relatively few layoffs and a low unemployment rate, is allowing many workers to continue spending.

The result is that fewer new rental units are becoming available just as more people are clamoring for them. National rents rose 2.7 percent in September, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index, compared with 2 percent a year earlier.

“Higher mortgage rates put pressure on the rental market not only from renters who are kind of stuck in there creating that demand,” said Molly Boesel, senior principal economist at Cotality, a housing market data provider. “But you also have that making it more difficult for builders to finance new apartments, so you could see a drastic slowdown in supply on the multifamily side.”

Most private rent indexes track new leases, which tend to adjust more quickly to market conditions. The rush of new apartment buildings in recent years, many of which reduced rents to lure tenants, caused rents in a number of cities to drop. Renters who renewed their leases continued to see their rents go up.

Lance Swank, the chief executive of the Sterling Group, a multifamily builder in Mishawaka, Ind., said his company had taken advantage of low interest rates to ramp up construction. When it became clear that a wave of new rental developments was about to inundate the market, his company decided to scale back.

“We became much more selective,” he said.

Mr. Swank, whose company builds and owns rental communities in the Midwest and Southeast, said he had also noticed the effects of rising mortgage rates on certain tenants. While renters in luxury apartments seemed less influenced by higher rates, fewer renters were moving out of his company’s lower-tier housing, he said.

“It’s just a math equation for people,” he said. “It’s what they can afford.”

It is not clear how much momentum the rental market is gaining. Yet the fact that it appears to be on slightly stronger footing at all has defied some economic projections.

Most notably, Stephen Miran, who served briefly as a Fed governor, said in a speech last year that he expected that the Labor Department’s measure of rent inflation would fall below 1.5 percent in 2027, from its level at the time of about 3.5 percent. One reason he cited was stricter immigration policy, which he believed would reduce the demand pressure on rents.

“One might characterize this view on rental inflation as optimistic,” he said in the speech. “However, I believe forecasters have underappreciated the significant impact of immigration policy on rent inflation — both on the way up and, now, on the way down.”

Complicating the picture for the Fed is a lag between moves in rental market data and government data. Typically, the Consumer Price Index, released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, takes time to catch up to market rents, partly because the government surveys any given rental property only once every six months. That means that if rent goes up the month after a survey, it will take another five months for it to show up in the data.

At the moment, however, rent inflation appears to be moving in step with market rents. One possibility for the alignment is that landlords are eager to raise rents, said Mark Franceski, the chief strategist at Middleburg, a developer of rental housing.

“Whether growth is flattening or accelerating, they seem to be moving in the same direction,” he said. “This is becoming less of a renters’ market and more of a landlords’ market.”

Forecasters broadly believe that the factors pressuring rents upward are not going away in the near term. The slowdown in residential building will limit housing availability. Mortgage rates, which are unlikely to fall substantially any time soon barring a recession, will keep pushing more people into the rental market.

“In theory, higher rates make it more restrictive: You slow growth, that lowers inflation,” said Chris Salviati, the chief economist at Apartment List.

“There is the counterargument that because you’ve got higher rates, you’re going to have less building, and then you’re going to have less supply,” he added. “And that will increase the pressure on shelter rents and make inflation worse.”

Siri Kahn, 32, pays $2,325 a month for a one-bedroom apartment on the North Side of Chicago. Though she and her husband have been saving money for 10 years to buy a home with enough room to start a family, they still can’t afford the down payment on a two-bedroom house in the city, she said. Moving to the suburbs would mean they would have to pay for gas to drive to their jobs instead of using public transportation.

While their most recent rent increase was manageable, they are bracing themselves for their rent to eventually rise above what they can bear.

“It’s only a matter of time until we are forced out of renting,” she said.

Since officials voted unanimously in September to raise rates by a quarter point to 3.75 percent to 4 percent, the incoming inflation data has been anything but reassuring. Energy prices are up across the board as the war with Iran has dragged on. The range of goods and services growing costlier appears to be broadening out. And a splurge in spending tied to the proliferation of artificial intelligence shows little sign of abating.

The Fed’s other priority, the labor market, has also remained stable, despite monthly growth downshifting in September, in a sign that the Fed’s policy settings are not excessively onerous for the economy.

Numerous Fed policymakers have already indicated their support for a rate increase at their final gathering of the year in December in pursuit of a “timelier” return to the 2 percent target after six years of overshooting it. So the question for Mr. Warsh at Wednesday’s news conference is, why wait?

“The economics support another rate increase,” said Loretta Mester, who ran the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland for a decade until 2024. “By not moving in October, I’m a little skeptical whether a timely path is substantially different from just being on a downward path to 2 percent.”

Mr. Warsh had the last word ahead of the upcoming rate decision. Speaking in Bangkok at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank this month, the chairman did little to change the narrative that had been laid out by a number of his fellow policymakers in the weeks prior. The overarching message was that the central bank had more work to do to tame inflation, but that there was no urgency to raise rates at consecutive meetings.

Among the officials to push for patience was John C. Williams of the New York Fed and Philip N. Jefferson, the vice-chair, both of whom are part of an internal policy-steering committee, known as the troika, that Mr. Warsh leads.

Those comments represented exactly the kind of guidance that Mr. Warsh had long denounced. Onstage in Bangkok. Mr. Warsh went so far as to say that it was a “new chapter at the Fed, and we’re not in that business anymore.”

But for a broad swath of economists and investors, the primary reason that a rate increase was not penciled in for October in the face of hotter-than-expected inflation data was precisely because of the steer that Mr. Warsh’s colleagues provided. What has also helped in the interim is recent jitters in financial markets amid concerns about the sustainability of the A.I. boom. That has made financial conditions, which measure the availability of credit in the economy, only slightly less accommodative than before.

But looking solely at the inflation data, Riccardo Trezzi, a former Fed economist who runs the research firm Underlying Inflation, said a rate increase was clearly justified on Wednesday.

“There is zero evidence of cooling down,” he said of current price pressures. Mr. Trezzi estimates that the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, which strips out volatile food and energy items, will reach 3.4 percent in December. At the same time last year, it stood at 3 percent. Overall inflation, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, is projected to reach 3.8 percent, according to Mr. Trezzi’s calculations, nearly double the 2 percent target. P.C.E. data for September will be out on Thursday, the day after the Fed’s decision.

“There’s a disconnect in terms of how the Fed sounds at the moment,” he said. “They still have to make up their minds whether they’re really serious about disinflating the U.S. economy.”

The issue for the Fed is that the primary sources of resurgent inflation are out of their control. Beyond the Iran war and Mr. Trump’s tariffs, both of which have bid up price pressures, many of the biggest A.I. companies that are fueling growth also appear impervious to higher rates.

Perhaps the biggest propellant of demand right now is the sharp rise in wealth across the country being generated from stock market gains, said Marc Sumerlin of Evenflow Macro, an economic consulting firm.

In the last four quarters, households’ net worth rose roughly $20 trillion, according to Fed data as of September. While most of these gains have accrued to high-income households, the bulk of consumer spending is driven by this group.

Estimates vary about how much the Fed will need to squeeze the economy in the coming months to begin to turn the tide on inflation. Some believe price pressures will begin to ease as the impact of Mr. Trump’s tariffs and the energy shock fade, obviating the need for an aggressive response from the Fed. But for others, a more forceful approach might be required.

“If you want to lower inflation now, you have to lower demand because raising supply takes time,” Mr. Sumerlin said.

The first of two wild cards is how financial conditions evolve in the coming months. U.S. government bond yields are sharply higher today than just a few months ago for a variety of reasons. Some of that reflects changing expectations about how much the Fed will need to raise rates as growth has picked up. There is also intensifying competition between governments and companies for capital as large A.I. companies borrow aggressively to fund their expansions.

Investors also appear to be demanding extra compensation to hold longer-dated debt versus shorter-term ones amid ever-present concerns about Washington’s fiscal profligacy and whipsawing worries about the Fed’s ability to operate independently, said Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist at Morgan Stanley Wealth Management.

Rising yields on the margins will help the Fed in its pursuit of its inflation goal, but that will not supplant entirely the work the central bank has to do when it comes to raising rates to at least a neutral level that neither speeds up nor slows down the economy, Ms. Zentner said.

The second wild card is how the public perceives the Fed’s grip on inflation. Concerns about price pressures in the year ahead have mounted, but longer-term metrics look more benign.

For now, that has afforded the Fed some flexibility around when it must deliver additional increases, said Raphael Bostic, who served as president of the Atlanta Fed for nine years until February. But, “there are limits,” he warned.

“The danger always is that every additional month that inflation is way higher than your target is another month where people say, ‘maybe this is the new normal,’” Mr. Bostic said.

True, much of the data pointed to strength, or at least stability. Retail sales rose at a healthy pace in September. Filings for unemployment benefits remained low. Industrial output hit a postpandemic high.

But there was no relief on the issue that matters most to many voters, inflation. Consumer prices rose last month at their fastest rate since May, outpacing wage growth for the sixth month in a row. Producer prices, too, came in hot, as did prices for imported goods. And gasoline — the most visible price in the economy, and one that few Americans have any choice about paying — stayed above $4 a gallon nationally, where it has been for most of the past six months.

Little wonder, then, that measures of consumer sentiment have worsened, and that polls show voters are poised to punish Republicans for failing to keep the economic promises they made on the campaign trail two years ago.

The cost of living “is going to be the first issue on the scorecard in 2026,” said John W. Lettieri, president of the Economic Innovation Group, which last week published a survey of voter attitudes on the economy. “The results are not good on that top issue.”

Still, the state of the economy is more nuanced than the dour mood of voters might suggest. Economists point to areas of weakness and others of strength, and say the outlook — for inflation and more broadly — is highly uncertain.

Affordability challenges go beyond inflation.

Wages vs. inflation

Inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index, had fallen to about 3 percent when Mr. Trump returned to office, from a peak of 9 percent in 2022. Most economists expected it to drop further.

Instead, progress stalled in 2025, partly because of Mr. Trump’s tariffs, which drove up prices of many imported goods. Then, just as the tariff effect was beginning to fade, Mr. Trump led the United States into war with Iran, which pushed energy prices and inflation back up. Consumer prices were up 3.7 percent in September from a year earlier.

“Voters had the sense that President Biden’s policies were leading to higher prices, and voters have the sense that President Trump’s policies are leading to higher prices now,” said Michael Strain, an economist at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank. “In both cases, I think voters made the right judgment.”

Gas prices are just the most visible piece of a broader affordability challenge. Record prices for diesel fuel are threatening to ripple through to food and other goods. The artificial intelligence boom has led to a surge in demand for computer chips and related equipment, which has raised costs for smartphones, tablets and other consumer electronics. And some economists say they believe companies are still waiting to pass along some of the cost of tariffs to customers.

Higher inflation has also forced the Federal Reserve to reverse course and begin raising interest rates again, which is making it more expensive to borrow money as many Americans are relying on debt to make ends meet. Mortgage rates have jumped this year, dashing hopes of a rebound in the housing market and pushing homeownership further out of reach for many families.

Then there is the other side of the affordability equation: income. Wage growth slowed to just 3 percent in September, down from nearly 4 percent a year earlier. The combination of higher prices and weaker earnings growth means that, at least by one measure, the average worker has experienced no wage growth, adjusted for inflation, since the beginning of Mr. Trump’s second term.

The labor market is solid, but stagnant.

Job turnover rates

American households, at least in the aggregate, have weathered higher prices better than many economists predicted. That is partly because the job market has held steady — workers may not be getting big raises, but at least most of them have jobs.

The unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent in September, remains low, and has been at or below 4.5 percent for five years — a record. Layoffs, despite fears of job losses from A.I., remain low by historical standards. Nearly 81 percent of adults of prime working age, 25 to 54, were employed in September, close to a 25-year high.

But while the labor market is solid, it is hardly robust. Companies are not cutting jobs, but they are not adding many, either — a “low-hire, low-fire” stasis that makes it hard for anyone who needs a job to find one. The average unemployed worker has been looking for a job for nearly six months.

The slow pace of hiring also makes it harder for people to change jobs, or threaten to, in search of higher pay. The rapid rate of job-switching after the pandemic, sometimes referred to as the “great resignation,” helped many workers keep up with higher prices. The slower pace of turnover now may be part of the reason wage growth has slowed. It is particularly hard on younger workers, who typically change jobs frequently as they seek a foothold on the career ladder.

“You have to scramble pretty hard to find another job that is better than your current job,” said Skanda Amarnath, executive director of Employ America, a research group focused on the labor market. “There’s a level of fragility in that. How am I supposed to feel like I can get ahead if I’m not earning a higher wage increase?”

Spending and investment depend on A.I.

Quarterly business investment

Strong retail sales data last week was the latest evidence that Americans are spending despite their dour mood. Consumer spending, adjusted for inflation, grew at a 3.8 percent annual rate in the second quarter, and most forecasters expect strong numbers for the third quarter as well.

Business investment, too, has been robust, with companies pouring money into equipment and software. Corporate profits continue to set records, helping to push the stock market — despite some jitters — to fresh highs.

But much of that strength stems from sectors connected to A.I., and the trillions of dollars in infrastructure needed to enable it.

Seemingly insatiable demand for microchips, data centers and the electricity to power them is responsible for much of the increase in investment. The companies that benefit from that demand, like Nvidia, the chipmaker, are helping to fuel the surge in corporate profits. And the market’s gains are helping to prop up consumer spending, especially among the wealthy households that own most stocks.

That could leave the economy vulnerable if investors lose confidence in the A.I. boom. There are hints that could already be happening. Shares of CoreWeave and other data center operators have tumbled amid questions about whether their enormous spending will ever pay off. In a research note published on Friday, Torsten Slok, the chief economist at Apollo Global Management, warned that a pullback in investor enthusiasm for A.I. could expose “a stagflationary environment in which growth slows even as price pressures persist.”

At the same time, a growing number of economists and technologists, including leaders of the A.I. companies themselves, are warning the technology could lead to widespread job losses. To many workers, that has created the impression that A.I. portends something of a Catch-22 for their well-being: If A.I. achieves its promise, it could put them out of work. If it falls short, the bursting bubble could wipe out their retirement portfolios and cause a recession.

“For two or three years, we have been waiting with bated breath for this A.I. bubble to pop or for this mass displacement to occur,” said Elizabeth Pancotti, vice president at Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive research organization.

That is adding to a more general sense of economic uncertainty that is eroding voters’ confidence. And it has been a long time since most Americans felt stable.

“The thing that people want more than anything, more than economic opportunity or economic growth, they want economic stability,” Ms. Pancotti said.

How Does the Economy Feel to You?

New York Times economics reporters want to understand how Americans are navigating employment and the rising cost of living. We may want to use your experience in a story, but we would only do so with your permission.

FinanceTab.title: Budget 2026 live: £100 energy payment for millions and rise in bank tax as watchdog warns on stalling living standards
FinanceTab.text:
OBR: living standards forecast to rise by just 1% over whole post-Covid decade

The OBR report says RHDI (real household disposable income – one measure of living standards) is rising at a record slow rate – less than 0.1% per decade. That means, by the end of the decade, it will be just 1% higher than its pre-Covid level, it says.

double quotation markOur central forecast represents a continuation of the historically weak growth in RHDI per person since the global financial crisis. Chart 2.7 shows the rolling 10-year average annual growth in RHDI per person. This slowed significantly in the aftermath of the financial crisis, due to lower growth in productivity and real wages. Growth reached a historic low over the 10 years to 2025-26, averaging just ¼ per cent a year, and we expect it to fall further in the near term. By 2029-30, our central forecast sees growth over the prior 10 years averaging less than 0.1 per cent a year. As a result, 10 years on from the onset of the pandemic, RHDI per person would be just 1 per cent higher than its pre-pandemic level.

Minister dismisses as 'garbage' Tory and Lib Dem claims that defence spending actually being cut

A Treasury minister has dismissed as “garbage” opposition claims that the small print in the budget book shows that John Healey is actually cutting defence spending.

The budget red book says that, while £42.6bn had been set aside for MoD spending in 2027-28, that has now been revised down to £41.1bn.

The Treasury says this is because less money than expected is needed for pensions. But James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, said that not allocating the unused money for other areas of defence spending was “a complete dereliction of duty from the chancellor”.

And James MacClearly, the Lib Dem defence spokesperson, made the same argument. He said:

double quotation markIt is disgraceful that after pitching Labour as serious on defence, Healey and [Wes] Streeting are cutting the military’s resource budget by nearly £1bn next year. This will leave our troops worse off and undermine our security.

In response, Torsten Bell, a Treasury minister, posted this on social media.

double quotation markAbsolute garbage - this is a technical change that happens when public sector pension contributions change. There’s no impact on defence spending power & the Tories used the same mechanism in govt. What does matter for defence spending? The chancellor, who has increased it

A 'picky bits' budget: What the economists say

Today’s ‘picky bits’ budget has pushed tough decisions into next year, says Tim Sarson, head of tax policy at KPMG UK:

double quotation mark“When it comes to tax rises, as expected with his options limited by the 2024 manifesto, the chancellor was left with a pick and mix or ‘picky bits’ approach.

Overall the announcements today will raise £7bn per year by 2031-32 with some winners and losers including a widely trailed bank surcharge, which came in lower than expected at 3% and further taxes on the gambling sector

James Smith, ING’s developed markets economist in the UK, says the budget has left more questions than answers.

Those questions include:

double quotation markHow will the government account for higher inflation in departmental budgets? How will it fund defence? Both questions were left unanswered today. The government’s overall spending pot for government departments was left largely unchanged later this decade, despite a higher path for inflation and the chancellor’s reaffirmed commitment to 3% Nato spending by 2030. Implicitly, that pledge is being funded by squeezing other areas of government; the OBR’s numbers imply real-terms cuts of 2.6% a year for unprotected departments later this decade.

That almost certainly won’t happen – and this is before you take social care or any of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s other bold policies into account.

These thorny issues have been punted into 2027, potentially in the autumn, when the government will have to unveil its long-awaited spending review.

The New Economics Foundation says the budget is a missed opportunity to bring down inflation, through more ambitious cost of living measures.

double quotation markThe chancellor has missed an opportunity to bring down inflation rates, according to analysis from the New Economics Foundation (NEF). The research suggests a more ambitious package of cost-of-living policies would take inflation from the OBR’s projected 3.64% to 2.88% by June 2027.

But Capital Economics say the chancellor has done enough to keep the markets on side.

double quotation markToday’s UK budget announcement has proven the non-event that newly-minted Chancellor Healey had signalled in advance. While his first budget is hardly inspiring, it contrasts favourably with the initial efforts of some of his recent predecessors.

By sticking to a gradual fiscal tightening path, and to the expectations set over the past couple of months for a muddle-through budget, Healey has probably done enough to keep the Gilt market on side for now.

We think that Gilt yields will fall over the coming year as the UK’s fiscal risk premium remains contained and the Bank of England policy takes a less hawkish path than money markets discount.

Updated at 17.50 GMT

Ministerial direction needed for £6.5bn loan for Ukraine after export finance agency warns of 'exceptionally high' risk of default

The government needed to issue a ministerial direction to get UK Export Finance to approve a £3bn increase in lending for Ukraine, it emerged today. This is a procedure that happens when a civil servant judges that a decision is not justified under normal responsible public spending rules, and insists that it can only go ahead if a minister explicitly overrules the objections.

In his letter explaining the need for a ministerial direction, Tim Reid, UKEF’s chief executive, argued that this was not a core obligation for the agency (which is there to help British exporters, not to fight Russia) and that the risk of the £6.5bn not being paid back was too high.

double quotation markUKEF has played a significant role in delivering the government’s support to Ukraine by staying on cover with £3.5bn of capacity to provide export finance, supporting strategically important transactions including the supply of nuclear fuel, reconstruction of critical infrastructure and air-defence missiles. These have supported Ukraine’s resilience at a critical time while also creating jobs and industrial capacity across the UK.

However, the financial risks associated with UKEF providing support in Ukraine remain far beyond those that we would normally be willing to accept. The probability of default and expected loss is exceptionally high …

UKEF is close to capacity against its existing £3.5bn limit. You have now asked me to consider a £3bn increase in UKEF’s cover limit, taking UKEF’s Ukraine country risk limit to £6.5bn.

In response, Jonathan Reynolds, the business secetary, said he was issuing a ministerial direction because “the United Kingdom has been steadfast in its support for Ukraine’s defence, economic resilience and long-term recovery, and I consider UKEF’s support to be an important component of that wider effort.”

Updated at 17.29 GMT

OBR: Employment Rights Act will have negative impact on economy

Labour’s Employment Rights Act is likely to have a negative impact on the economy, the OBR says today.

This is the first time that the OBR has assessed the potential economic impacts of the ERA, which received royal assent at the end of last year.

And the fiscal watchdog has concluded the ERA will probably have a negative impact on potential output, though it isn’t making an explicit assessment today.

double quotation markOur analysis suggests that the ERA will likely have a negative economic impact from negative impacts on businesses, particularly through increased uncertainty, lost flexibility and higher labour related costs, which will more than offset any potential positive impact on worker productivity.

That fits with the government’s own analysis, which said the reforms could cost businesses up to £5bn a year.

Updated at 17.30 GMT

How budget includes £10bn in extra support for Ukraine

Earlier John Healey got an endorsement for what he said about defence spending from Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general. (See 2.15pm.)

George Robertson, the former Nato secretary general and the lead author of the strategic defence review, has also welcomed Healey’s defence announcements. (See 1.30pm.) He said:

double quotation markJohn Healey is acting in the national interest – and has done exactly what he said was needed for defence in his resignation letter, by setting a headmark for 3% in 2030.”

I am strongly in favour of innovative ways of financing defence – and this is a credible route to get more into UK defence. Today’s annoucements strengthens UK leadership in Nato once again.

In his speech Healey announced an extra £10bn in economic support for Ukraine. This Treasury news release explains where that money is going. It says:

double quotation markThe £10bn package includes £7bn of economic support being made available over three years, including up to £5.5bn of World Bank guarantees and a £500m grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association’s crisis facility, mobilising £1.5bn of support for Ukraine.

Alongside this, there will be a £3bn increase in UK Export Finance (UKEF) capacity for Ukraine, prioritised for military support. It will bring the total UKEF support to £6.5bn.

Updated at 17.00 GMT

Over at Saxo UK, traders report there was little drama in today’s budget.

“It was a boring budget” says Andrew Bresler, the chief executive of Saxo UK, adding:

double quotation markThey have been able to achieve what they set out to which is effectively no movement in financial markets.

Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at the bank, says the budget was “a nothing burger”, pointing out:

double quotation markThe market is not really reacting to it.

More here.

Updated at 17.01 GMT

What business organisations are saying about budget

Business groups have given the budget a mixed reaction.

Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the CBI, welcomed some measures, but argued John Healey should have done more for growth. She said

double quotation markOn the face of it, this budget lacks the bold moves that would have made it easier for firms to invest, hire and grow.

At a time of exceptional geopolitical pressures, using some fiscal headroom to absorb genuine short-term shocks is preferable to loading additional permanent costs onto business and weakening investment.

Slowing the convergence of youth rates with the national living wage is a sensible move in face of the Neets crisis and current labour market pressures. But the chancellor could have gone further. Reducing the cost of hiring by increasing the employer NICs threshold would have given firms more space to create entry-level jobs and boost employment.

Jonathan Geldart, director general at the Institute of Directors, said his members were relieved.

double quotation markBusiness leaders will be relieved that the chancellor’s budget included no nasty surprises, having been conditioned in previous budgets to expect the worst. We very much welcome the numerous measures intended to support British start-ups and scale-ups, such as the new Founders’ Relief, Young Entrepreneurs Allowance and EMI2 [enterprise management incentive] share incentives (as well as support for small brewers).

What might at first blush be a case of small beer today could start adding up to something promising in the future.

But Tina McKenzie, national chair of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), said the budget was a disappointment.

double quotation markThis budget should have been the moment to help small businesses with the soaring costs holding them back, and the taxes restricting job creation. Instead, they got nothing to ease sky-high energy bills and nothing to make hiring someone more affordable, while the increase in business rates relief excludes too many.

Kalyeena Makortoff

A JP Morgan spokesperson has criticised the decision to hike the UK’s bank tax today, arguing that targeting one of the UK’s most lucrative sectors “lacks principle”:

double quotation mark“We are committed to the country, and we recognise the cost of living challenges there and the global economic headwinds that it faces, but to single out this industry for additional taxes again, one of the UK’s biggest generators of growth and jobs, lacks principle.

“It also overlooks that the banking industry operates in a highly competitive global marketplace.”

But despite the bank’s disappointment, JP Morgan is due to charge ahead with its £3bn new UK HQ, according to a source familiar with the matter.

More in our business live blog.

Updated at 16.46 GMT

What opposition parties are saying about the budget

Kemi Badenoch’s reaction to the budget on behalf of the Conservative party was covered earlier, at 2.11pm. Here is some reaction from other oppostion parties.

The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, told MPs that John Healey should have done more to address the problems with Brexit. He said:

double quotation markI do think this budget will be more defined by Labour’s red lines on Europe and the Conservatives’ Brexit red tape, rather than faster growth.

And at the root of so much of what’s gone wrong in our country – the cost of living crisis, higher taxes, broken public services, empty high streets, the lack of jobs and opportunity – at the root of all of that is the lack of economic growth.

Our economy is being held back. British business is being held back, and it’s been held back above all by the terrible damage of the Conservative Brexit deal.

Ellie Chowns, the Green party Treasury spokesperson, said the budget was lacking in ambition.

double quotation markYou’d have thought that, after going to the trouble of ousting the last PM, taking his job, and installing a brand-new chancellor, Andy Burnham would be keen to ensure Labour displayed a bit more ambition at today’s budget than it did under his predecessor.

Unfortunately, what Britain actually saw today was a business-as-usual budget which failed to engage with the real issues facing our country – choosing to tinker round the edges, rather than properly taxing extreme wealth and profits, making essentials genuinely and permanently affordable, or investing in our long-term climate resilience.

There was no discussion of the climate crisis in Healey’s speech today, nor any new investment in renewables and climate adaptation, despite the devastating impact of this summer’s deadly heatwaves and wildfires on our communities, public services, and economy.

Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said Britain was broke. In a post on social media, he said:

double quotation markThese are the stats John Healey doesn’t want you to read.

Unemployment will rise to 5% in 2027.

The tax burden is going up AGAIN to the highest since WW2.

By 2031 we’ll be spending £160bn/year on debt interest alone – up £36bn/year …

We are on a fiscal knife-edge. Britain is Broke. Britain needs Reform.

Kirsty Blackman, the SNP’s economy spokesperson at Westminster, said this was not a budget for Scotland. She said:

double quotation markThe UK Budget shows the Labour government doesn’t get Scotland – and isn’t doing anywhere near enough to protect people from the looming cost of living emergency this winter.

This isn’t a budget that a Scottish chancellor would have delivered. Instead of providing meaningful help, it has abandoned families in the face of soaring bills and has imposed another betrayal on Scotland’s energy – with the decision to scrap Scottish carbon capture funding.

Andy Burnham promised to cut the cost of living but every major household bill has increased on his watch – and the UK budget completely fails to address the scale of the challenge families are now facing.

Ben Lake, Plaid Cymru’s economic spokeperson at Westminster, said Wales was just an afterthought in the budget.

double quotation markToday’s budget was UK Labour’s opportunity to prove that Wales is more than an afterthought in Treasury decisions. Instead, it appears to have delivered the worst funding settlement for Wales in years.

After months of promises about a new relationship with Wales and a new approach from the Treasury, the question many people will be asking is – where is the ambition

The chancellor chose not to announce what Wales would receive in consequentials from this budget. Buried in the documents is around £450 million of additional funding spread over three years. That falls well short of keeping pace with inflation and risks forcing the kind of spending reductions Wales experienced during the worst years of Tory cuts.

Updated at 16.47 GMT

UK gambling firms' value jumps after chancellor resisted large duty hike

Machine games duty (MGD) is the tax levied on slot machines found in bookmakers, casinos, bingo halls and adult gaming centres (AGCs). The chancellor faced calls to double the rate of MGD from 20% to 40%, a policy backed by one of his predecessors, Gordon Brown.

Amid fierce lobbying from gambling firms, which issued dire warnings of thousands of job cuts, Healey opted for a more modest rise to 25% today. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.

Investors responded with relief, adding £240m to the combined stock market value of Entain (Ladbrokes/Coral), Evoke (William Hill), Rank Group (Mecca Bingo/Grosvenor Casinos) and Playtech (designer of slot machine games). Entain said the MGC hike will cost it £25m, which it expects to be able to mitigate, including by shop closures. Betfred boss Fred Done, whose family took a £30m dividend from their betting empire earlier this year, also warned that closures and job losses would follow.

The chancellor singled out AGCs, sometimes known as “slot farms” for particular attention. As well as the duty rise, they will also be excluded - along with vape shops - from business rates relief available to retail and hospitality businesses.

Updated at 16.16 GMT

Burnham rules out general election in the next year

Andy Burnham has ruled out calling a snap general election in the next year amid ongoing speculation (including among economists and investors) that he could seek to consolidate his position.

He said he was thinking “about people” and not “my own party and its prospects”, Press Association reports.

The prime minister was asked if he would call an election in the next year as he visited a community centre in central London after the Budget.

double quotation mark“I don’t know how many times I’ve done this now, but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months.

“I have said repeatedly since coming into this job, I’m not thinking about myself. I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects.

“I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them to have that care for people, which I spoke about on my first day in Downing Street.”

He added that he was “leading from the front” and “putting Britain on a different path”.

double quotation mark“We’ve got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage.”

Updated at 16.46 GMT

City experts: Risk of an early election

Several City economists are suggesting that today’s budget may be teeing up an early general election.

Andrew Wishart, senior UK economist at Berenberg, suggests there is a 40% chance of a general election before the end of 2027.

He points out that this would allow Labour to discard its previous manifesto commitments not to raise taxes on working people.

double quotation markThe big questions, about how to fund a national social care service and a £15bn increase in defence spending by 2030 remain unanswered. The government will hope that the combination of a decline in gilt yields a reduction in transfer payments to those with disabilities and efficiency savings enable them to fund their priorities without a major increase in taxes. It’s just about possible, but pretty unlikely and requires tax hikes pencilled in for the back end of the parliament to come in, potentially just before the next general election.

More ambition would require a new mandate without the manifesto constraint on tax, achieved by via a general election. We put the chances of one before the end of next year at about 40%.”

Eoin O’Callaghan, macro strategist at Wellington Management, says there is a “significant question mark” over the credibility of the projections, including the biig squeeze on departmental spending in a few year’s time.

double quotation markLike last autumn’s budget they incorporate an unrealistic real term freeze in departmental spending in 2029-30, after the next election. And they now incorporate an even more challenging 3% real terms cut to next year’s departmental spending too to help offset rising interest rate and unfunded public sector pensions costs. The forecasts are also predicated on nominal growth staying relatively elevated close to 4% throughout the forecast.

“That may not concern the market for now. But it highlights how challenging the UK public finances are. How difficult the fiscal decisions ahead of this government are. And why there is a risk of early elections given the tough spending decisions ahead.”

Benjamin Jones, Invesco’s Global Head of Research, predicts speculation about an early election will continue to build:

double quotation mark“After two blockbuster, tax-hiking budgets, investors will welcome this more ‘steady as she goes’ package from the new Labour Chancellor. Against a backdrop of rising gilt yields and geopolitical uncertainty, Healey’s decision to limit spending increases and tax rises shows sensible caution.

His opening comments were clearly aimed to ease bond market fears. However, many of the difficult fiscal choices - such as delivering welfare savings and boosting Defence spending - have been postponed until the Spending Review next year, which will continue to fuel speculation of an early election.

How proposed first-time buyer Isa will work

John Healey announced a first-time buyer ISA in his speech. This is what the Treasury says about how it will work.

double quotation markThe government will introduce a new FTB ISA from April 2029. The product will replace the Lifetime ISA (LISA) for new savers and provide a 25% government bonus, paid on withdrawal, towards the purchase of a first home worth up to £450,000. The maximum value of the bonus will be capped at £20,000. Existing LISA holders will be able to continue contributing to and using their accounts under the current rules. In addition, the government will reduce the withdrawal charge for existing LISA holders who use their savings to purchase a first home above the £450,000 property price cap.

SportsTab.title: Manchester United: Michael Carrick and Bruno Fernandes hold clear-the-air talks
SportsTab.text:
Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick and captain Bruno Fernandes have held clear-the-air talks before the team's trip to Chelsea.

Fernandes, 32, was an unused substitute during United's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth on Sunday.

The Portuguese was dropped to the bench after he criticised Carrick's tactics following the 4-1 loss against Como in the Champions League.

Sources have told BBC Sport that the pair spoke privately at the club's training ground on Tuesday, with the talks aimed at airing issues.

It is unclear whether Fernandes, who was made club captain in 2023, apologised for his critical comments.

United are preparing for Saturday's trip to Chelsea (12:30 GMT), when Fernandes could return to the starting line-up.

Carrick was widely expected to be sacked following the Bournemouth game, but he will take charge of the Premier League match at Stamford Bridge.

United's board decided the 45-year-old deserved the opportunity to turn things around at Old Trafford, despite the team languishing in 16th place in the Premier League.

There was further good news for Carrick on Wednesday, with midfielder Kobbie Mainoo returning to training after a fortnight out through injury.

Despite managing just one victory in eight Premier League matches this term, the predicament at the club is not seen as being entirely Carrick's fault by the board.

Senior figures at the club feel United's players - a squad they think are capable of qualifying for the Champions League - are underperforming badly and should shoulder some blame.

One player told BBC Sport: "The feeling is that we all want to put it right. Players, staff, everyone."

Nevertheless, sources have told BBC Sport that the club have shortlisted former Newcastle United boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany and Bayern Munich head coach Julian Nagelsmann as potential replacements for Carrick.

Any decision to appoint Howe would trigger a multi-million-pound compensation claim from his former club Newcastle, while Nagelsmann is a free agent.

SportsTab.title: South Africa vs Australia: Marnus Labuschagne hits record low but new guard stand up for tourists
SportsTab.text:
Third Test, Cape Town (day two of five)

South Africa 329: Ackerman 95; Starc 6-72

Australia 330-4: Inglis 85*; Jansen 2-37

Australia lead by one run

Marnus Labuschagne has been front and centre for an era of Australian cricket.

Chirping, chewing and, with bat in hand, often appearing to idolise and mimic his team-mate Steve Smith.

Smith has been ruled out of the enthralling decisive Test against South Africa with a neck injury.

Without him, Australia wanted their number three to feast at last chance saloon, where he has been perched for an eternity, on day two in Cape Town.

The 32-year-old lasted five deliveries and did not score a run.

Labuschagne failed to scored a Test century for the 48th time in a row - a new record for the number of innings an Australian top order batter has waited to raise his bat at three figures.

"That will never be broken," said former Australia quick Jason Gillespie on ABC.

"I say that because, respectfully, I don't think anyone will be given that length of time again."

There was a time when, from his insertion into the 2019 Ashes as a concussion substitute until the end of England's next quest to win back the urn, Labuschagne averaged 65 in Test cricket.

Repeat that over a Test career and only Sir Donald Bradman's mark of 99.94 would be ahead.

Instead, since his last Test century at Old Trafford in 2023, he averages 24.77.

Labuschagne may get one more chance in this Test, should Australia not progress from their position of 330-4, leading by one run, and dismiss South Africa before needing to pad up again.

Even that may not be enough.

"I just feel it is too far gone now," Gillespie added. "It is a very big sample size. Australia are at a point where they need to look elsewhere."

Labuschagne's technique has been pored over again and again as his slump progressed.

In August, the great Ricky Ponting, one of his predecessors as Australia's number three, called for the axe to fall.

"He can't score off the back foot," was Ponting's cutting remark.

Having batted nicely in three or four innings in this series only to give it away after reaching 30, here he was stuck on the crease, playing back to a full ball and nicking spinner Simon Harmer to slip.

"That's nerves and the pressure the selectors have put him under for an extended period of time," said former Australia batter Simon Katich on SEN Radio.

"They put him in this position by not making the decision to give him a breather."

It felt like all of Labuschagne's issues collapsing into one.

But if his pained stare down the pitch signalled the end of something, what followed hinted at their future.

With Travis Head already out and Labuschagne following, the score 58-2 in reply to the Proteas' 329, there was no Smith to steer Australia out of this tricky spot.

Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green and Josh Inglis, three of the junior members of this side, instead made fifties and put their side in the ascendancy.

Renshaw is one of those who has been kept out by the selectors in the hope Labuschagne could rediscover his best form.

Had he been picked to open in the World Test Championship final against South Africa in 2025, rather than Australia's decision to try Labuschagne as opener, he may have spent the following 17 months ending the debate over who should replace David Warner.

Having got his chance in this series, initially as number five before the Nic Maddinson experiment was cut short after two Tests, the Middlesbrough-born Renshaw looks like being a fixture for this winter and beyond.

His 74 here, which followed a career-best 190 in Durban, suggests a return to England next summer awaits.

Green is one who has not lacked opportunity. Long viewed as Australia's golden boy, the 27-year-old has flicked across 39 previous Test without ever truly appearing comfortable.

In making 65 below Table Mountain, the towering all-rounder played with the composure and authority he has often lacked.

Most impressive, though, was Inglis - another Aussie who spent his early years in Yorkshire.

He had not faced the red ball since March, has had his preparations limited by a broken finger, and came in with South Africa buoyed by Marco Jansen dismissing Renshaw and Green in successive overs before tea.

The 31-year-old finished 85 not out in an unbroken partnership of 145 with Alex Carey. There would be no late-evening South Africa fightback, like the one Mitchell Starc inspired on day one to bowl South Africa out.

This is not to say everything has fallen into place for Australia. Smith will return, meaning Green and Inglis would likely move from their current batting positions of four and five for their next Test against New Zealand in December.

Smith has avoided batting in Labuschagne's position before, and a four-Test trial of Green in that spot in 2024 and 2025 was aborted after he returned 188 across eight innings.

Leeds-born Inglis, meanwhile, has three first-class matches worth experience at number three, in which he averaged 12.66 and has a best score of 29.

But if ever a day showed Australia there is merit in moving from one generation to another it was this.

Three of their less experienced players, albeit two of them have celebrated their 30th birthdays, stood up to take Australia to a position from which they can control this Test.

Labuschagne did not. His days look numbered.

SportsTab.title: Arsenal to appeal against Max Dowman's red card against Fleetwood in Carabao Cup
SportsTab.text:
Arsenal will appeal against Max Dowman's sending-off during Tuesday's Carabao Cup tie at Fleetwood.

The 16-year-old midfielder was shown a straight red card in the 85th minute after reacting to a heavy challenge by Fleetwood's Harrison Neal.

Although Dowman did not fully kick out, his foot did make contact with Neal.

The game finished 1-1 before League Two Fleetwood beat the Premier League champions 5-3 on penalties.

It was Dowman's second red card this month having also been sent off while representing England's Under-19s.

As Dowman left the field, Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta gave him a scathing look and made what appeared to be an angry comment to the young winger.

Arteta said after the game: "When we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to respect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate. It was very clear."

Dowman was dismissed for violent conduct, which according to the laws of the game is when a player "uses or attempts to use excessive force or brutality against an opponent when not challenging for the ball... regardless of whether contact is made".

As it stands, Dowman will face a three-match suspension.

The Gunners were already light on options on the wing as Bukayo Saka, Christos Tzolis and Noni Madueke are currently out injured.

SportsTab.title: Thierry Henry responds to backlash over Ballon d'Or comments
SportsTab.text:
Thierry Henry has defended himself after criticism over the way he hosted Monday's Ballon d'Or ceremony.

The former France and Arsenal forward, who has come under fire for remarks he made towards Barcelona star Lamine Yamal, overall winner Harry Kane and co-host Kate Scott on the night, has addressed what he said was "people getting really excited about nothing".

Henry, who was presenting the ceremony alongside CBS Sports colleague Scott, joked with Lamine Yamal about him winning a third successive young player of the year award.

He also corrected Scott's pronunciation of Brazil legend Socrates' name and admitted he wanted fellow Frenchman Kylian Mbappe to beat Kane to the top prize.

Addressing the Lamine Yamal situation, which received an audible reaction from the audience in attendance, Henry said he wasn't "checking his ego" and emphasised his admiration of the young Spaniard.

On the night, he teased Lamine Yamal by saying of his young player award: "It's your third one, right? But is it the one you really wanted to win?"

Speaking in a social media video on Wednesday, Henry said: "I'm a big fan of Lamine Yamal. I wasn't checking his ego at all - that you didn't like the joke, I can understand.

"But don't do that, he's one of the players I'd pay to watch, I love him."

The 49-year-old also responded to criticism over his response to co-host Scott's pronunciation of 'Socrates', claiming she was in on the joke herself.

"You didn't like the joke, I understand, but please stop saying I disrespected Kate," Henry said.

"I will never do that and you can ask her, she was on the joke with me. She did Soc on purpose, and I said Soc, so please stop inventing stories."

Arsenal forward Bukayo Saka won the Socrates Award for his humanitarian and charity work.

Henry added Kane was a "worthy winner" of the Ballon d'Or before telling everyone to "relax" after his support of Mbappe's claim to the prize.

"I'm French and I was always going to back up and support my fellow countryman," he said.

"I said to [Kane], 'You are a worthy winner, you deserve it, you are the example that work ethic is a talent, working hard is a talent'. Well done, Harry Kane - and I call him Sir Harry Kane since the World Cup.

"So please, people out there, relax, relax. I love Harry Kane, I love Lamine Yamal and I didn't disrespect Kate. She was on the joke with me."

SportsTab.title: Sergio Perez signs multi-year extension with Cadillac
SportsTab.text:
Sergio Perez will remain with Cadillac until 2029 after signing a multi-year contract extension.

The 36-year-old, who is set to celebrate his 300th Grand Prix start in his home race in Mexico City this weekend, joined the American Formula One team last August before their debut season on the grid, racing alongside fellow veteran Valtteri Bottas.

Perez made his Formula One debut in 2011 and has won six grands prix – five for Red Bull between 2021-24 and one for Racing Point (now Aston Martin) in 2020.

He finished third in the 2022 drivers' championship and second behind team-mate Max Verstappen in 2023.

Despite having two years left on his contract, he was dropped by Red Bull at the end of the 2024 season after the team felt he had run out of time to prove he could support Verstappen.

Perez sits bottom of the 2026 standings, with three 14th-place finishes – in Barcelona, Silverstone, and Azerbaijan – his best performances. Neither he nor Bottas has earned a point for Cadillac.

"Joining Cadillac from day one was a project I truly believed in, and extending my commitment feels like a natural continuation of this chapter," said Perez.

"Building a Formula One team from the ground up takes time, relentless work and patience, but the progress we are making together is incredibly rewarding.

"There is still a lot of work ahead of us and I am fully committed to the next three years."
